deep.reconstruction:
Context: this sheet is not a Riemann autograph. It is an editor's fair copy, probably Hattendorff's or Weber's, of a short example taken from Riemann's Nachlass. It is headed 'XXVI. Beispiel einer Fläche vom kleinsten Inhalt' and was evidently prepared for printing with Riemann's Werke. The struck-out preamble says so explicitly: the example 'unter Riemann's Papieren ... enthalten ist' and 'dürfte der Mittheilung werth sein'. The references to 'Art. 13' and 'Art. 14 der Abhandlung über die Fläche vom kleinsten Inhalt' point to Riemann's posthumous paper 'Über die Fläche vom kleinsten Inhalt bei gegebener Begrenzung' (ed. Hattendorff, 1867).

Problem. Find the minimal surface bounded by three straight lines that meet pairwise in two points. The surface then has two corners and one sector running off to infinity. Let α, β, γ be defined by the angles απ, βπ, γπ between the lines.

Step 1 (Gauss map). Along a straight boundary line the surface normals lie in a plane, so they trace a great circle on the sphere. The spherical image of the surface is therefore a spherical triangle with angles απ, βπ, γπ. Hence α+β+γ > 1 (spherical excess).

Step 2 (parametrization). Map the surface conformally to the upper t-half-plane. The two corners go to t=a and t=b, and the infinite sector goes to t=c. Following Art. 13, the auxiliary function u (Riemann's log-type variable) is
 u = ∫ C dt / ( sqrt((t-a)(t-b)) (t-c) ).
Its closed form is
 u = -(1/2) log[ (sqrt((t-a)/(c-a)) - sqrt((t-b)/(c-b))) / (sqrt((t-a)/(c-a)) + sqrt((t-b)/(c-b))) ].
By my check, differentiating gives du/dt = sqrt((c-a)(c-b)) / ( 2 (c-t) sqrt((t-a)(t-b)) ), i.e. C = -sqrt((c-a)(c-b))/2. Thus u is the arctanh of a ratio of square roots. It has a logarithmic singularity at t=c, which corresponds to the infinite sector.

Step 3 (normalization). Put a=0, b=∞, c=1; the factor sqrt(t-b) is absorbed into the constant. Then
 du/dt = 1/(2(1-t)√t),  u = -(1/2) log((1-√t)/(1+√t)) = artanh √t.

Step 4 (the function k, Art. 14). The Gauss-map coordinate η is to be written as a quotient k1/k2 of two solutions of a linear second-order equation. In the variable u, chosen with 'v = u', that equation has no first-derivative term. The page gives
 (1/k) d²k/du² = -(1/t)(1/4-α²) - t(1/4-β²) - α² - β² + γ² + 1/2.
Using d/du = 2(1-t)√t d/dt (my step), one gets d²k/du² = 4[ t(1-t)² k'' + (1/2)(1-t)(1-3t) k' ]. This turns the u-equation into the t-equation
 t(1-t)² k'' + (1/2)(1-t)(1-3t) k' + (1/4) k [ (1/4-α²)/t + (1/4-β²) t + α² + β² - γ² - 1/2 ] = 0.

Step 5 (Riemann P-function). The t-equation is a Riemann (Papperitz) equation with singular points 0, ∞, 1:
 k = P{ 0: 1/4 ± α/2 ; ∞: 1/4 ± β/2 ; 1: ±γ/2 ; t }.
I verified this against the standard Papperitz form with these exponents:
- the exponent sum is 1, as the Fuchs relation requires;
- the exponent differences are α, β, γ, matching the triangle angles απ, βπ, γπ at 0, ∞, 1.
The shift by 1/4 at t=0 and t=∞ is exactly what removes the first-derivative term in the u-variable. η is then the quotient of any two particular solutions; this is the Schwarz-type triangle map onto the spherical triangle. The minimal surface itself would follow by Riemann's integral formulas from η and u; that step is not carried out on the page.
errors: No mathematical errors found. All displayed formulas check: the general u-integral and its log closed form (with C = -sqrt((c-a)(c-b))/2), the special case a=0, b=∞, c=1, the u-form of the k-equation, its t-form, and the P-symbol (Fuchs relation and exponent differences).
Minor imprecision: the constant in u = ∫ const dt/... is left unspecified, and for b=∞ the factor sqrt(t-b) is silently absorbed into the constant. This is harmless.
The phrase 'wenn man v = u annimmt' depends on notation in Riemann's Art. 14 that is not reproduced here, so its exact meaning cannot be checked from this page alone.

results.what: Spherical (Gauss-map) image of a minimal surface bounded by straight lines is a spherical polygon of great-circle arcs; here a triangle with α+β+γ>1
results.modern_name: Gauss map / Schwarz–Riemann method for Plateau problem with polygonal boundary
results.usually_credited_to: Riemann (Minimalflächen paper, publ. 1867) and Schwarz (1865 onward)

results.what: u = ∫ dt/(sqrt((t-a)(t-b))(t-c)) = artanh-type closed form; special case u = artanh √t
results.modern_name: Elementary integral (logarithmic singularity at an end of the polygon)

results.what: η as quotient of solutions of a Riemann P-equation with exponents (1/4±α/2, 1/4±β/2, ±γ/2), normalized so the u-equation has no first-derivative term
results.modern_name: Schwarz triangle function / hypergeometric (Riemann P) representation of a conformal map onto a spherical triangle

results.what: Explicit example: minimal surface bounded by three lines meeting in two points (two corners, one infinite sector)
results.modern_name: Riemann's example of a minimal surface with polygonal boundary (published in Riemann's Werke from the Nachlass)

deep.surprise_reason: This is an editor's fair copy of a Nachlass example that was published in Riemann's Werke. Its methods (Gauss map onto a spherical triangle, P-functions) are those of Riemann's own published minimal-surface paper. Nothing here is unknown or anachronistic; it only confirms a published attribution.

transcription_corrections: The hand is an editor's fair copy (Hattendorff/Weber), not Riemann's autograph. The struck preamble refers to 'Riemann's Papieren' in the third person.

'für [?] welches' in the struck preamble: the '[?]' is a deleted or illegible word. The phrase 'ohne eine ausreichende Andeutung' is uncertain in the image and may read differently, e.g. 'nur mit einer kurzen Andeutung'.
In the angle sentence, the deletions are '$\alpha,\beta,\gamma$' replaced by '$\alpha\pi,\beta\pi,\gamma\pi$'; the final inequality reads α+β+γ > 1. The transcription is essentially correct here.
The insertion after 'Inhalt' is a bracketed page reference '(S. ...)' left blank for the printer. This is consistent with preparation for the Werke edition.
